items.stem: How many dimensions of human security did the 1994 Human Development Report identify?
items.answer: Seven
items.markingKey: Seven. Economic, food, health, environmental, personal, community and political security.

items.stem: Distinguish between freedom from fear and freedom from want.
items.answer: Freedom from fear concerns protection from violence and conflict; freedom from want concerns protection from poverty, hunger and disease – the two pillars of human security.
items.markingKey: Freedom from fear concerns protection from violence and conflict; freedom from want concerns protection from poverty, hunger and disease – the two pillars of human security. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain why securitisation can be dangerous.
items.answer: Framing an issue as an existential threat allows governments to bypass normal democratic processes and rights, as with some counter-terrorism laws after 2001 or restrictions on migrants.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Framing an issue as an existential threat allows governments to bypass normal democratic processes and rights, as with some counter-terrorism laws after 2001 or restrictions on migrants. (3 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: "Human security means that military security is no longer important." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Human security broadens rather than replaces security; protection from violence (freedom from fear) is central, and military capabilities may be needed to provide it.
items.markingKey: Human security broadens rather than replaces security; protection from violence (freedom from fear) is central, and military capabilities may be needed to provide it. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem:
Source D
Security is about survival. It is when an issue is presented as posing an existential threat to a designated referent object, justifying the use of extraordinary measures to handle it.
— Barry Buzan, Ole Wæver and Jaap de Wilde, Security: A New Framework for Analysis (1998) (paraphrased)

Outline three points made in Source D about traditional and human security. [3]
items.answer: security is about survival; an issue is presented as an existential threat to a referent object; this justifies extraordinary measures
items.markingKey: Award 1 mark for each of the following, up to [3]: security is about survival; an issue is presented as an existential threat to a referent object; this justifies extraordinary measures. Points must be drawn from the source; accept close paraphrase. Own knowledge is not credited.

items.stem: "The broadening of the concept of security has been harmful." Discuss.
items.answer: Broadening has benefits, but securitisation must be used cautiously to avoid undermining rights.

items.stem: Explain why the concept of security expanded after the Cold War.
items.answer: With the decline of superpower confrontation, threats such as civil wars, famine, HIV/AIDS and environmental degradation became more visible; most victims of insecurity were individuals within states, so security was redefined around people.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: With the decline of superpower confrontation, threats such as civil wars, famine, HIV/AIDS and environmental degradation became more visible; most victims of insecurity were individuals within states, so security was redefined around people. items.stem: Briefly explain why a state can be secure while its people are not.
items.answer: A state may face no external military threat but its citizens may suffer repression, poverty, crime or disease; in some cases the state itself is the main threat to its people.

items.stem: Using the Ottawa Treaty banning anti-personnel landmines (1997) as an example, explain human security in practice.
items.answer: A coalition of NGOs (the International Campaign to Ban Landmines) and middle powers such as Canada achieved a treaty now joined by over 160 states; the campaign won the Nobel Peace Prize. The treaty prioritised protection of civilians over military utility, reflecting a people-centred concept of security.

items.stem: Evaluate the claim: "Human security is more relevant than traditional security in contemporary global politics."
items.answer: Both are relevant; human security captures most everyday threats, but traditional threats have returned to prominence.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: most deaths come from intrastate conflict, poverty and disease; pandemics and climate change threaten people across borders; R2P reflects people-centred security. Arguments against: Russia’s invasion of Ukraine revived interstate military threats; rising defence spending ($2.7 trillion in 2024); states remain the main providers of security. Supported judgement: Both are relevant; human security captures most everyday threats, but traditional threats have returned to prominence. items.stem: Explain why food security is a political as well as an economic issue.
items.answer: Access to food depends on prices, trade, conflict and government policy; blockades (Yemen, Gaza), export bans and war (Ukraine 2022) can create hunger, and food price spikes contributed to unrest such as the Arab Spring in 2011.

items.stem: "Cyber attacks are carried out only by criminals." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: States and state-sponsored groups carry out many major attacks (Stuxnet, NotPetya), alongside criminal ransomware groups.
items.markingKey: States and state-sponsored groups carry out many major attacks (Stuxnet, NotPetya), alongside criminal ransomware groups. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Outline one way in which the Colonial Pipeline ransomware attack (May 2021) shows cyber threats to critical infrastructure.
items.answer: A criminal group, DarkSide, shut down the largest fuel pipeline on the US East Coast; the company paid a ransom of about $4.4 million. A non-state criminal group disrupted national infrastructure, showing how cyber threats blur crime and national security.
items.markingKey: Context (A criminal group, DarkSide, shut down the largest fuel pipeline on the US East Coast; the company paid a ransom of about $4.4 million.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. items.answer: cyberspace is a domain of operations; it is equivalent to land, sea and air; a serious cyber attack could trigger Article 5

items.stem: Explain the difference between cyber espionage and cyber attack.
items.answer: Cyber espionage steals information without necessarily causing damage (e.g. the SolarWinds hack, 2020); a cyber attack disrupts or destroys systems (e.g. NotPetya, 2017).

items.stem: Using Russian gas supply cuts to Europe (2022) as an example, explain energy security as a political weapon.
items.answer: Russia reduced supplies through Nord Stream 1 before the pipelines were damaged in September 2022; the EU cut its dependence on Russian pipeline gas from about 40 per cent to under 10 per cent. Energy dependence gave Russia leverage, prompting the EU to diversify suppliers (LNG, Norway) and accelerate renewables.

items.answer: The world produces enough food; hunger results mainly from poverty, conflict, prices and unequal access.

items.stem: Examine the view that non-traditional security threats require multilateral rather than national responses. Use relevant key concepts and named examples in your answer. [15]

items.answer: Once, after the attacks of 11 September 2001

items.answer: Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022 transformed threat perceptions; public opinion swung towards membership, and Article 5 offered a guarantee that neutrality could not.

items.stem: Distinguish between disarmament and arms control.
items.answer: Arms control limits and regulates weapons to reduce risk; disarmament aims to reduce or eliminate weapons entirely, as the TPNW does for nuclear weapons.

items.answer: After decades of military non-alignment, Finland joined NATO, doubling the alliance’s land border with Russia. Russia’s invasion of Ukraine produced the very NATO enlargement it opposed, showing how alliances respond to perceived threats.

items.stem: Hana writes: "NATO is a collective security organisation like the UN." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: NATO is a collective defence alliance of specific members against external threats, not a universal system against any aggressor.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "deterrence"?
options: An arrangement in which members commit to defend each other if attacked, as in Article 5 of the North Atlantic Treaty (1949)
The process, described by the Copenhagen School (Buzan, Wæver), by which an actor presents an issue as an existential threat to justify extraordinary measures
A people-centred approach to security that includes “freedom from fear” and “freedom from want”, introduced in the UNDP Human Development Report 1994
Preventing an attack by threatening unacceptable retaliation, especially with nuclear weapons
items.answer: Preventing an attack by threatening unacceptable retaliation, especially with nuclear weapons
items.markingKey: D. "deterrence" is preventing an attack by threatening unacceptable retaliation, especially with nuclear weapons.

items.stem: Explain the difference between collective defence and collective security.
items.answer: Collective security is a universal system in which all states act against any aggressor (UN); collective defence is an alliance of particular states committing to defend each other against external attack (NATO).

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "referent object"?

items.stem: Give one argument for and one argument against this view: "Non-traditional security threats require multilateral rather than national responses."
items.answer: Non-traditional threats need multilateral cooperation, though national capacity remains essential.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: pandemics and climate cross borders; cyber crime requires international cooperation (Budapest Convention); food markets are global. Arguments against: states retain responsibility and capacity; multilateral institutions are slow and divided; national resilience (energy diversification) works. Supported judgement: Non-traditional threats need multilateral cooperation, though national capacity remains essential.

items.stem: Evaluate the claim: "Arms control has no future in an era of great-power rivalry."
items.answer: Arms control is in crisis, but rivalry has historically motivated rather than prevented arms control.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: collapse of INF, suspension of New START; China’s nuclear expansion without limits; new technologies outpace treaties. Arguments against: arms control was negotiated during the Cold War rivalry; shared interest in avoiding nuclear war; TPNW and NPT norms persist. Supported judgement: Arms control is in crisis, but rivalry has historically motivated rather than prevented arms control. items.stem: "The broadening of the concept of security has been harmful." To what extent is this view justified?
items.answer: Broadening has benefits, but securitisation must be used cautiously to avoid undermining rights.

items.stem: Which report first set out the concept of human security in 1994?
items.answer: The UNDP Human Development Report
items.markingKey: A. It identified seven dimensions: economic, food, health, environmental, personal, community and political security.

items.stem: Which agreement of July 2022, brokered by Türkiye and the UN, allowed Ukrainian grain exports through the Black Sea?
items.answer: The Black Sea Grain Initiative
items.markingKey: A. Russia withdrew in July 2023.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "A system in which all states agree to act together against any aggressor, as envisaged by the UN Charter (Chapter VII)"?
items.answer: collective security
items.markingKey: B. This is the definition of collective security.

items.stem: Jonas writes: "Human security means that military security is no longer important." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Human security broadens rather than replaces security; protection from violence (freedom from fear) is central, and military capabilities may be needed to provide it.
items.markingKey: Human security broadens rather than replaces security; protection from violence (freedom from fear) is central, and military capabilities may be needed to provide it. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Amara writes: "Food insecurity is caused mainly by a global shortage of food." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: The world produces enough food; hunger results mainly from poverty, conflict, prices and unequal access.
items.markingKey: The world produces enough food; hunger results mainly from poverty, conflict, prices and unequal access. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: "Nuclear arms control has eliminated the risk of nuclear war." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Arms control reduced arsenals from a peak of about 70,000 warheads in 1986 to about 12,000 today, but nine states still possess nuclear weapons and key treaties have collapsed.
items.markingKey: Arms control reduced arsenals from a peak of about 70,000 warheads in 1986 to about 12,000 today, but nine states still possess nuclear weapons and key treaties have collapsed. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain the difference between traditional security and human security.
items.answer: Traditional security focuses on the state as the referent object and military threats from other states; human security focuses on individuals and a wide range of threats, including poverty, disease and repression.
items.markingKey: Traditional security focuses on the state as the referent object and military threats from other states; human security focuses on individuals and a wide range of threats, including poverty, disease and repression. items.stem: Distinguish between cyber espionage and cyber attack.
items.answer: Cyber espionage steals information without necessarily causing damage (e.g. the SolarWinds hack, 2020); a cyber attack disrupts or destroys systems (e.g. NotPetya, 2017).

items.stem: Distinguish between collective security and collective defence.
items.answer: Collective security is a universal system in which all states act against any aggressor (UN); collective defence is an alliance of particular states committing to defend each other against external attack (NATO).

items.stem: Using the securitisation of HIV/AIDS (UNSC Resolution 1308, 2000) as an example, explain the broadening of the security agenda.
items.answer: The Security Council for the first time addressed a health issue as a threat to international peace and security. Framing a disease as a security threat mobilised resources and attention, showing how securitisation can expand the agenda.
